original_question: How can heterogeneous crystal nucleation be simulated atomistically for increasingly realistic interfaces, including the interfacial detail needed for reliable force fields, while still extracting general trends that are not tied to a single material system?
target_in_paper: In light of the literature we have reviewed in here, we believe that much of the effort has to be devoted in the future to i) enable atomistic simulations of heterogeneous nucleation dealing with increasingly realistic interfaces and to ii) obtain general, maybe non material-specific trends able to point the community into the right direction, even at the cost of sacrificing accuracy to a certain extent.
correct_elements: Identifies the need for atomistic simulations of heterogeneous nucleation with realistic interfaces and the goal of extracting general non–material-specific trends.
missing_details: Clarify that ‘realistic interfaces’ include atomistic features such as substrate defects, impurities, and interfacial structure
State that the force fields must be extremely transferable and reliable to capture interfacial detail
Mention that classical molecular dynamics with improved interatomic potentials is the intended simulation framework
Include the trade-off of ‘sacrificing accuracy to a certain extent’ to achieve generality
Specify that the goal is to derive non–material-specific nucleation trends
Quantify that this refers to heterogeneous crystal nucleation in supercooled liquids
refined_question: What strategies can be developed to perform classical atomistic molecular dynamics simulations of heterogeneous crystal nucleation in supercooled liquids that (a) incorporate increasingly realistic substrate–liquid interfaces—including atomistic defects, impurities, and accurate interfacial force field parameters—and (b) extract general, non–material-specific nucleation trends even if this requires sacrificing some force field accuracy?
justification: The refined question restates verbatim the dual objectives enumerated in Section III of the paper: enabling atomistic simulations of heterogeneous nucleation with realistic interfaces (including defects and transferable force fields) and obtaining general, non–material-specific trends at the expense of some accuracy. It remains narrowly scoped to heterogeneous nucleation in liquids and uses the paper’s terminology without broadening beyond the authors’ intent.
